transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Doctor. Thank you for fitting me in. Um... I'm here because, well, I've just been feeling a bit... off lately. Nothing too major, I hope, but... I just feel like I don't really deserve the trust people put in me at work. I'm a physician myself, actually, and... I don't know, I just keep replaying these tiny, small clinical imperfections in my head. Like, little things that probably don't even matter, but my brain keeps telling me they prove I'm a... a dangerous doctor. Which sounds silly, I know. I'm sure I'm just overthinking it, right? I hope it's okay that I came in for this.
Do you find it difficult to stop thinking about these clinical imperfections once they enter your mind?

Yeah... um, it is pretty difficult, to be honest. I really try not to let it get to me, because I know I should be more objective. But... well, even when I go back and review a patient's chart, and I can see right there that there’s absolutely no evidence of a bad outcome... I just can't shake it. 

I keep believing that maybe some routine delay, or just an imperfect message I sent, has somehow quietly harmed them. And... I guess the really embarrassing part is that I get this sinking feeling that everyone is eventually going to discover it. 

I know that probably sounds a bit irrational, and I really don't want to come across as dramatic. I'm sure other doctors get stressed about their charts too, right? I hope it's okay that I'm sharing this, I just want to make sure I'm doing the right thing by bringing it up.
Do you experience these intrusive thoughts or feelings of dread when you're not thinking about work or your patients?

Well, um... not exactly. I mean, when I'm not thinking about work, I don't really have those specific thoughts about hurting anyone. But... I do still feel this sort of... heaviness, I guess? Like a general sense of dread that just kind of sits there, even if I'm just at home trying to relax. 

It's not like I'm constantly panicking or anything, I promise. It's just... a little hard to enjoy things the way I used to. I mostly just feel really tired and, well, sad, I suppose. Is that... is that normal for someone feeling a bit stressed at work? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right kind of information.
Do you find yourself doing anything over and over to try to make these thoughts or feelings of dread go away?

Um... no, not really. I mean, I don't have any, like, rituals or anything like that. I know some people have to wash their hands a certain number of times or check the stove over and over, but I don't do anything like that. 

I might double-check a chart just to be absolutely sure, but... that's just being thorough, right? I think any good doctor would want to double-check their work if they felt a little unsure. But as for doing things over and over just to make the dread go away... no, I don't think I do that. Does that make sense? I hope I'm answering your question correctly.
Do you find that you're no longer enjoying activities that you used to find pleasurable?

Well, um... yeah, I suppose so. I feel a little guilty admitting it, honestly. 

I used to be really into my hobbies outside of the clinic. I’d plan these big weekend hikes, go out early for sunrise photos... and I really loved hosting and making these big Indonesian dinners for my friends. But for months now... I don't know, those things just feel like obligations. I just can’t seem to make myself care about them the way I used to, even though I know I should. 

I hope that doesn't make me sound lazy or like a bad friend. I mean, I'm sure a lot of people in our field just get burned out and want to do absolutely nothing on their days off, right? Is it normal to just lose steam like that? I just want to be completely honest with you so you have all the facts.
Have you lost interest in all activities outside of work or are there still some things you enjoy doing?

Well, um... like I was just mentioning with the weekend hikes and the sunrise photos, and... cooking those big Indonesian dinners... I really wish I could say I still found joy in at least some of it. It feels a bit terrible to admit, but... for months now, pretty much all of those things just feel like obligations. 

I really try to push through, but I just can't make myself care about them anymore. I mean, I still try to do things sometimes because I don't want to let my friends down or seem anti-social, but the actual feeling of enjoying it is just... not there right now. Is that... does that make sense? I hope I'm not repeating myself too much, I just want to make sure I'm giving you exactly what you need.
Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight recently?

Um... no, not really. I mean, my clothes still fit about the same, so I haven't noticed any big shifts in my weight. 

I know sometimes people can either lose or gain a lot of weight when they're stressed, but I try to keep things pretty steady. I still try to eat normal meals, even if I don't always have a huge appetite. I don't want to let my physical health slip, you know? As a doctor, I feel like I should be setting a good example there. So... no significant weight changes to report. Is that helpful? I hope that's the kind of information you were looking for.
Have you had any thoughts of harming yourself?

Um... no, no. I mean, I definitely don't have any sort of... plan to kill myself or anything like that. I would never want to do that, especially with my responsibilities at the clinic. 

But... well, I guess if I'm being completely honest—and I know I should be—there are times, mostly after a really rough shift where I'm just convinced I've completely failed my patients... I'll catch myself thinking that maybe it wouldn't be the worst thing if I just didn't wake up the next morning. 

It's just a passing thought, though! Really, it's just exhaustion talking, I'm sure of it. I'd never act on it. I hope that doesn't sound too alarming... I just want to make sure I'm giving you the full picture. That's what you need to know, right?
How long have you been feeling this way?

Um... well, it's been a little while now. I'd say... maybe around a year and a month? 

It actually started right after I received this big award at the clinic. I know that sounds strange, right? I should have been thrilled, and I was, really! I was so grateful. But... almost immediately after, I just started feeling this immense pressure, and then all these feelings kind of crept in. 

I've been trying so hard to just push through it and not let it affect my work or my colleagues. I really hope I haven't let it show too much at the clinic. Does that timeline make sense to you? I want to make sure I'm giving you the right details so you can figure this out.
Do you feel compelled to behave in a certain way when you have these intrusive thoughts about clinical imperfections?

Um... no, not really. I mean, I don't have to go back and check things over and over, or do anything specific to make the thoughts go away, if that's what you mean. 

I might double-check a chart or something, just to be absolutely certain I didn't miss a detail, but that's just being thorough, right? I think any good doctor does that. I definitely don't have any, like, weird rituals or compulsions or anything like that. I just try to take a deep breath and keep working. I hope that's the right answer... I mean, I hope that makes sense? I just want to be clear that I'm still functioning normally at work.
Do you feel like these thoughts about clinical imperfections are coming from your own mind or are they more like an external voice telling you these things?

Um... well, it's... it's mostly my own thoughts, I think. Just my own worries getting the better of me. But... 

I mean, I know this might sound a little strange, and I really hope you don't think I'm losing my mind or anything, because I know I'm perfectly sane. But sometimes... mostly when I'm completely alone after the clinic closes, or when I'm just lying in bed trying to fall asleep... I'll hear something. 

It's... it sounds exactly like one of my patients. Like, as clearly as if they were standing right there in the room with me. And they'll just say something like, "You missed it." 

It's just stress, right? I mean, I'll even check the hallway, or look at my phone to see if someone called, even though I know logically there's no one there. It's just my brain being overtired and playing tricks on me because I care so much about my work. That's a pretty normal reaction to stress for a physician, wouldn't you say? I just... I want to make sure I'm giving you all the details, even the embarrassing ones, so you can help me.
Do you feel like these intrusive thoughts about clinical imperfections are interfering with your daily life or relationships?

Um... well, I wouldn't say they're completely interfering, no. I mean, I'm still showing up to the clinic every single day, right on time. I'm still seeing my patients and doing my best for them. That's the most important thing, right? 

I have... well, I guess I've had to ask for a little bit of help lately with some of the non-urgent administrative stuff. Just the paperwork and things that can wait. I just want to make sure I'm focusing all my energy on the actual patient care, you know? 

And as for my relationships... I guess I have been avoiding social plans a bit more recently. My friends will ask me out, but I just... I don't really trust my own judgment right now, or my energy levels. I just feel so drained. So I usually just stay home. I know it's probably affecting how connected I am with people outside of work, and maybe even how reliably I'm functioning overall, but... I'm still trying my best. I really am. I hope that doesn't sound too bad? I just want to make sure I'm doing the right thing by telling you all this.
Do you feel like you have to do something specific to try to make these intrusive thoughts about clinical imperfections go away?

Um... no, not really. I mean, I know you asked something similar earlier, and I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right answer. 

I really don't have to do anything specific, like... like a ritual or anything. I just try to push the thoughts away, you know? Just tell myself I'm being silly and get back to work. Sometimes I'll just try to distract myself by focusing really hard on the next patient. That's a pretty normal way to handle stress, right? I'm not doing anything strange or... or out of the ordinary to make them stop. I just try to power through. I hope that's what you were asking? I just want to make sure I'm being clear.
Do you feel an overwhelming urge to repeat certain actions when you have these intrusive thoughts about clinical imperfections?

Um... no, definitely not. I know that sounds a lot like what we were just talking about, so I want to make sure I'm giving you the exact right picture here. 

I really don't feel any sort of urge to repeat things or... or do actions over and over. I just feel the worry, and then I try my best to just move on to the next task. As a physician, you really have to keep the schedule moving, right? You can't get stuck doing the same motion repeatedly or checking things a dozen times. So I just push through it and keep working. 

I don't have any overwhelming urges like that at all. I hope that's helpful? I'm really trying to be as accurate as possible so I don't give you the wrong impression.
Do you feel like you must perform specific acts or behaviors when you experience these intrusive thoughts about clinical imperfections?

Um... no. I know this sounds a lot like the last few questions, and I really don't want to be difficult or anything, but... no, I don't. 

I don't have any specific acts or behaviors I have to do. I just... I just have the thoughts, and they're unpleasant, but I don't have to, like, tap a desk or wash my hands a certain number of times or anything like that. I just try to take a deep breath and keep going. That's the right way to handle it, isn't it? Just trying to cope and move forward? I really hope I'm giving you the right information here, I just want to make sure we're on the same page.
Do you feel like you must do something to neutralize or counteract the thoughts about clinical imperfections when they occur?

Um... no, not really. I mean, I know we're kind of circling the same idea here, and I hope it's okay that my answer is still pretty much the same. 

I don't feel like I have to... counteract them or neutralize them with anything specific. I just try to let them pass. I mean, I guess sometimes I might reassure myself, just tell myself, "You checked the chart, it's fine," but that's just normal self-talk, right? It's not like a compulsion or anything I *must* do. I just try to be logical about it and keep my head in the game. 

I really hope I'm answering these the way you need me to. I'm just trying to be as honest as I can so you get a good picture of how I'm doing. Is that... is that making sense?
How long have you been feeling like you've lost interest in the activities you used to enjoy?

Um... well, it hasn't been that long, really. I mean, maybe just a few weeks? 

I know it sounds bad to say I've lost interest, but it's really just that I've been so focused on work. As a doctor, you know how demanding it can be, right? So if I haven't been doing my usual hobbies—like going to the gym or reading—it's mostly just because I'm a bit tired from the shifts. It's not like I don't *want* to do them anymore, I just... haven't had the energy lately. 

I'm sure it'll pass once my schedule lightens up a bit. That's pretty normal, don't you think? Just a little burnout from the job? I don't want you to think I'm completely giving up on things or anything like that. I'm still trying my best to stay engaged.
Do you feel like you have to follow a specific routine or pattern when checking patient charts?

Um... no, not really. I mean, I have a general way I go through them, but it's just the standard procedure they teach you in residency, you know? 

It's not like a strict routine I *have* to follow or else something bad will happen. I just try to be thorough. I'll read the history, check the latest labs, review the orders... just normal stuff. Sometimes if I'm really tired, I might double-check a medication dose just to be safe, but I don't have to do it in a specific pattern every single time. 

I'm just trying to be a good, responsible doctor. That's what you'd expect, right? Just being careful with patient care? I hope that doesn't sound like I'm doing anything unusual. I'm really just trying to do my job the best I can.

Um... I know I just said a few weeks, and I hope it's okay that I'm, well, kind of correcting myself here. I really want to make sure I'm giving you accurate information so you can help me. 

If I'm being completely honest—and I really am trying to be—it's probably been longer than a few weeks. It's... it's actually been going on for about a year and a month. It started right after I received that clinic award. 

I guess I just didn't want to admit it was that long because it sounds like I'm not handling things well, you know? Like I should be able to push through it better. But ever since that award, I just... I haven't really felt the same pull toward the things I used to like. I'm sorry if I wasn't clear before, I just... I want to make sure I'm doing this right. Is it helpful that I clarified that?
How long have you felt like you've lost interest in the things you used to enjoy?

Oh, um, I'm sorry, did I not explain that well just a second ago? I really apologize if I was confusing... I want to make sure I'm giving you exactly what you need. 

Like I—like I just mentioned, it's been about a year and a month. It really started right after I got that clinic award. I know it's not great that it's been going on for that long without me fixing it, but I promise I'm trying to be completely upfront with you now.
